title: Compiler vs interpreter vs runtime
description: Learn the differences between compilers, interpreters, and runtimes, and when each is used.

data.text: Every programming language needs a way to turn human-written code into something the CPU can execute. Some use compilers, some use interpreters, and many use both together with a runtime environment. Understanding the differences helps you pick the right tool and debug performance issues.

A compiler reads your entire program, checks it for errors, and produces a standalone file of machine code — usually called an executable or binary. You can run this file anytime without the compiler present. Because the compiler sees the whole program, it can optimize aggressively.

data.title: Compiling C with GCC
data.content: GCC reads main.c, compiles it, and outputs a binary called main.

data.title: Compilation advantage
data.text: Compiled programs often start faster because the hard translation work is already done. The trade-off is that changing code requires recompiling.

An interpreter reads and executes your program one statement at a time. It does not produce a standalone executable. Instead, the interpreter must be present every time you run the program. This makes distribution easier but execution typically slower than compiled code.

data.title: Running Python with the interpreter
data.content: The Python interpreter reads main.py and executes each line.

data.text: A runtime environment sits between the compiled intermediate code and the CPU. Java and C# both compile to an intermediate bytecode. At runtime, a virtual machine (JVM for Java, CLR for .NET) converts bytecode to machine code using Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation. This balances startup speed with long-run performance.

cards.title: AOT Compilation
cards.description: Translates the entire program before it runs. Produces a standalone executable.

cards.title: JIT Compilation
cards.description: Translates code during execution. Can optimize hot paths based on actual usage patterns.

data.text: How Modern Languages Mix These Approaches

data.title: Language execution strategies
items: C and C++ — compiled to native machine code with no runtime required
Python — interpreted by CPython with optional JIT in PyPy
Java — compiled to bytecode, JIT-compiled by the JVM
C# — compiled to IL, JIT-compiled by the CLR runtime
JavaScript — JIT-compiled by the browser or Node.js engine

data.caption: Execution strategies across languages
data.definition:
graph TB
    S[Source Code] --> C[Compiler]
    C --> E[Executable]
    E --> R[Runtime]
    R --> M[Machine Code]
    S --> I[Interpreter]
    I --> E

items.question: Is interpreted code slower than compiled code?
items.answer: Usually yes, because the interpreter must analyze each line at runtime. However, JIT compilers can close much of this gap for long-running programs.

items.question: Does the .NET runtime replace the compiler?
items.answer: No. The C# compiler still produces IL. The runtime then JIT-compiles IL to machine code when the program runs.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Compilers produce standalone executables ahead of time
Interpreters execute source code line by line at runtime
Runtimes add services like garbage collection and JIT compilation
Modern languages often blend compilation and interpretation
data.takeaway: Knowing how your language executes helps you write faster, more predictable code and choose the right deployment strategy.
